children: The United States and eight partner countries have agreed to identify and safeguard artificial intelligence technologies and supply networks exposed to risks involving China, the Financial Times reported Sunday.

For investors, the pact signals closer coordination over infrastructure underpinning the AI industry. That could influence where companies build facilities, source equipment and commit capital, although the report didn't detail specific restrictions or funding commitments.

Japan, Australia, Israel, the United Kingdom, South Korea, India, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have signed, U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg told the FT. Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to join next week.

“The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it and the port that ships it can all be in different countries,” Helberg told the FT. “What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility.”

The agreement advances Pax Silica, Washington’s effort to deepen cooperation on AI supply chains as competition with China intensifies. It precedes President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
The agreement comes as a scandal involving former Nvidia

CEO Jensen Huang fuels bipartisan demands for tighter U.S. controls on AI chip exports. U.S. officials suspect a woman linked to Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to influence Nvidia to make advanced chips more available to China, the Associated Press reported, citing The New York Times. Beijing has denied the espionage allegation.

The fallout could increase pressure for restrictions affecting Nvidia’s access to Chinese customers. Proposed Senate measures would allow Congress to review advanced AI chip export licenses, authorize chip tracking to detect diversions and require allies to match U.S. export restrictions on Chinese chipmakers, the AP reported.

title: U.S., allies agree to coordinate AI supply chain security
